newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's Sandinista chief Ortega denies he ill.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's Sandinista chief Ortega denies he ill.

text.p: Nicaragua's former Sandinista president Daniel Ortega denied reports on Wednesday that he was suffering from a terminal illness, saying he had nothing more than a treatable heart condition.
"They've spoken of cancer, AIDS, leukaemia ... what haven't they mentioned," Ortega joked in an interview with Reuters, referring to local news reports.

Now 52, Ortega led the Sandinista revolution to triumph in 1979 and ruled Nicaragua for 11 years, fighting a bitter war with U.S.-backed contra rebels before losing power in a surprise election upset in 1990.

Still a major political figure, he fought and lost another presidential election in October 1996 to right-winger Arnoldo Aleman. Despite rumours that the Sandinista challenge would be strong, Aleman won by a 13.3 percentage-point margin.

Ortega said his only ailment was a heart problem dating back a couple of years that had happened because of high cholestrol levels. "They found an injury, a heart attack in the lower part of my heart," he said.

Ortega's heart attack was officially reported by the left-wing Sandinistas in 1995 in a brief statement but rumours about his health multiplied during the 1996 election campaign -- something he blamed on political enemies.
"I know who wants me dead," he said. "There's no point in answering them. I've never thought like that, I have quite a thick skin in that sense."

The former president has been under treatment since his heart attack. He is prescribed a special diet, exercise and medicines and flies two to three times a year to the Sandinistas' former sponsor, Cuba, for treatment.
This, together with his visible loss of weight, has led to rumours about a hidden illness.
"For people here, a healthy person is a fat or burly person," Ortega said. "On the other hand being thin is linked to starving of hunger or being ill."
"I feel quite good, better than many people who are not even aware of their real state of health," he added.

Nevertheless during the interview it was clear that the man who once harangued crowds of thousands and ran six miles (10 km) a day dressed in battle fatigues had adopted a quieter, less strenuous lifestyle.
Despite Ortega's heart problem and double election defeat, the Sandinistas have not shown signs of wanting a change of leader.
Ortega said his party never discussed the topic because "the leadership of the Sandinistas is determined by their weight in Nicaragua" rather than by the personality of a leader.
Asked how much longer he would stay as Sandinista leader, Ortega replied simply, "Let's see."
Pressed further, he said, "I don't really think in terms of dates, I have never thought in terms of dates, I don't think life is lived in dates, I just live it and that's it."
